hook: Engineers are turning common silk into high-performance plastic for 6G networks.

sections.voiceover: Engineers are turning common silk into high-performance plastic for 6G networks.
sections.visual_cue: Macro shot of shimmering silk fibers transitioning into a clear, rigid composite material.
sections.sfx_cue: High-frequency digital hum that transitions into a clean, resonant chime.
b_roll: Close-up of silk threads on a loom
Digital animation showing silk protein structure

sections.voiceover: Imperial College London, the University of Michigan, and Tufts University led this breakthrough silk research. How can organic silk fibers handle the massive data demands of future 6G networks?
sections.visual_cue: Map highlights of the three universities, followed by a schematic of a high-pressure heating chamber.
sections.sfx_cue: Low mechanical rumble increasing in pitch.

sections.voiceover: But creating this plastic-like composite requires heating silk fibers between 257 and 419 degrees Fahrenheit.
sections.visual_cue: Digital gauge needle climbing rapidly to 419 degrees Fahrenheit.
sections.sfx_cue: Sharp, metallic clicking of a pressure gauge.
b_roll: Thermal camera footage of a heating element

sections.voiceover: Researchers fuse these silk threads under 1900 to 9800 atmospheres to preserve the protein's crystalline structure. Imperial College London researchers found this silk twists terahertz light frequencies for high-speed 6G data encoding.
sections.visual_cue: Animation showing light waves twisting as they pass through the silk-based composite.
sections.sfx_cue: Soft, rhythmic pulses of digital data transmission.

sections.voiceover: This extreme pressure transformation makes silk a high-performance material for future 6G telecom networks.
sections.visual_cue: A single transparent sheet of the silk-plastic material held against a light source.
